issues.issue: Notice must be "in writing or in such form as may be acceptable to the Company," a standard fixed by one party alone with no criteria. Notice is also "deemed ... effectively given when mailed," without stating a method of mailing or proof of dispatch.

The saving of rights runs against "you or any other person," an unbounded class in a two-party agreement with no third-party obligations. Its relation to the forfeiture grounds it preserves rights alongside is left unstated.

Any "interpretation, construction or application" by the Company in its "sole and absolute discretion" is declared "final, binding and conclusive for all purposes," without saying whether this ousts judicial review or is merely subject to good faith. That is the term that decides whether the Company's forfeiture determinations under §2(c) can be contested.

The clause binds and benefits only "each successor and assign of the Company," saying nothing of the employee's heirs and successors, whom the opening paragraph makes parties and to whose estate §2(a) directs payment. A court could be asked whether the omission of the employee's side is deliberate (expressio unius) or must yield to those provisions.

The sentence "[a]ny liability of the Company to any person with respect to a benefit under this shall be based solely upon any contractual obligations that may be created hereunder" omits its noun after "under this," leaving the scope of the limitation unclear. Whether it reaches liabilities beyond the Payment cannot be read off the text.

The Company may "amend or terminate this Agreement at any time," which cannot be squared with §1's promise to pay $60,300 at the end of the Retention Period unless the savings clause for "benefits or rights to which you are otherwise entitled ... immediately prior" is read to protect an unvested Payment. A court would have to decide what, if anything, the employee is "otherwise entitled" to before the Retention Period ends.

Forfeiture follows if you "disclose or threaten to disclose" information, a trigger left undefined and reaching statements short of actual disclosure. The carve-outs (spouse, accountant, tax advisor, lawyer, or as required by law) also do not say whether disclosure in litigating this Agreement is permitted.
